title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: When the countess heard that Natasha was ill, she went to Moscow with Petya and the rest of the household, though she wasn't fully recovered herself and was still weak. The whole family moved from Marya Dmitrievna's house to their own and settled in town.

Natasha's illness was so serious that, fortunately for her and for her parents, everything that had caused it — her conduct and the breaking of her engagement — receded into the background. She was so ill that they couldn't consider how far she was to blame for what had happened. She couldn't eat or sleep, she grew visibly thinner and she coughed, and the doctors made them feel she was in danger. They could think of nothing but how to help her. Doctors came to see her singly and in consultation, talked a great deal in French, German and Latin, blamed one another, and prescribed a great variety of medicines for every disease they knew. But it never occurred to any of them that they could not know the disease Natasha was suffering from, just as no disease of a living person can be known. Every living person has his own peculiarities and always has his own peculiar, personal, new, complicated disease, unknown to medicine — not a disease of the lungs, liver, skin, heart, nerves and so on, as listed in medical books, but a disease made up of one of the countless combinations of the ailments of those organs. This simple thought could not occur to the doctors (just as it cannot occur to a wizard that he is unable to work his spells) because the business of their lives was to cure, they were paid for it, and they had spent the best years of their lives on it. Above all, though, that thought was kept out of their minds by seeing that they were really useful, as they truly were to the whole Rostov family. Their usefulness did not depend on making the patient swallow substances that were mostly harmful (the harm was hardly noticeable, since the doses were small). They were useful, necessary and indispensable because they met a mental need of the invalid and of those who loved her — and that is why there are, and always will be, pseudo-healers, wise women, homeopaths and allopaths. They met the eternal human need of those who suffer for hope of relief, for sympathy, and for something to be done. They met the need seen in its most elementary form in a child, who wants a hurt place rubbed. A child bumps itself and runs at once into the arms of its mother or nurse to have the sore spot rubbed or kissed, and it feels better once that is done. The child cannot believe that the strongest and wisest of its people have no remedy for its pain, and the hope of relief, together with its mother's sympathy as she rubs the bump, comforts it. The doctors were useful to Natasha because they kissed and rubbed her bump. They assured her it would soon pass if only the coachman went to the chemist's on the Arbat and got a powder and some pills in a pretty box for a ruble and seventy kopeks, and if she took those powders in boiled water at intervals of exactly two hours, neither more nor less.

What would Sonya, the count and the countess have done, how would they have looked, if nothing had been done? If there hadn't been those pills to give by the clock, the warm drinks, the chicken cutlets and all the other details of life prescribed by the doctors, whose carrying out gave the family circle something to do and some consolation? How would the count have borne his dearly loved daughter's illness if he hadn't known that it was costing him a thousand rubles, and that he wouldn't grudge thousands more to benefit her? If he hadn't known that, should her illness go on, he wouldn't grudge yet other thousands and would take her abroad for consultations there? If he hadn't been able to explain in detail how Metivier and Feller had failed to understand the symptoms, but Frise had understood them, and Mudrov had diagnosed them even better? What would the countess have done if she hadn't been able, now and then, to scold the invalid for not strictly obeying the doctor's orders?

"You'll never get well like this," she would say, forgetting her grief in her annoyance, "if you won't obey the doctor and take your medicine at the right time! You mustn't trifle with it, you know, or it may turn into pneumonia," she would go on, taking great comfort in saying that foreign word, which was incomprehensible to others and to herself too.

What would Sonya have done without the glad awareness that she hadn't undressed for the first three nights, so as to be ready to carry out all the doctor's instructions exactly, and that she still stayed awake at night so as not to miss the right time for giving the slightly harmful pills in the little gilt box? Even to Natasha herself it was pleasant to see that so many sacrifices were being made for her, and to know that she had to take medicine at fixed hours, though she declared that no medicine would cure her and that it was all nonsense. And it was even pleasant to be able to show, by disregarding the orders, that she didn't believe in medical treatment and didn't value her life.

The doctor came every day, felt her pulse, looked at her tongue and joked with her, paying no attention to her grief-stricken face. But when he had gone into another room, where the countess hurried after him, he put on a grave air. Shaking his head thoughtfully, he said that although there was danger, he had hopes of this latest medicine and they must wait and see; that the illness was mainly mental, but... And the countess, trying to hide what she was doing from herself and from him, slipped a gold coin into his hand and always went back to the patient with a calmer mind.

The symptoms of Natasha's illness were that she ate little, slept little, coughed, and was always low-spirited. The doctors said she couldn't manage without medical treatment, so they kept her in the stifling air of the town, and the Rostovs did not go to the country that summer of 1812.

She swallowed many pills and took drops and powders from the little bottles and boxes, of which Madame Schoss, who was fond of such things, had made a large collection. She was also deprived of the country life she was used to. In spite of all that, youth prevailed. Natasha's grief began to be covered over by the impressions of daily life, it stopped pressing so painfully on her heart, it gradually faded into the past, and she began to recover physically.
